news.title: Investors temper Anthropic IPO valuation expectations after Q3 growth slows
news.summary: After Anthropic's investor day, prospective buyers are reportedly talking about a roughly $1.5 trillion valuation for its November listing, down from about $2 trillion. Q3 revenue rose 45% to $16.8B, a slower pace than the near-doubling in Q2.

news.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
news.summary: Speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt, Amjad Masad said Replit dropped Anthropic over cost, partnership and performance, claiming OpenAI models now build apps better. People familiar with the relationship disputed that the partnership had ended.

news.title: Meta launches Muse Spark Open, an open-weight model that runs on Macs
news.summary: Meta released open weights for Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter model with a 1M-token context that it calls the most capable US open-weight model. It targets local Apple silicon, though it needs around 1 TB of RAM.

news.title: Elorian's first model, Glimpse, reasons with images instead of just about them
news.summary: Palo Alto startup Elorian opened API access to Glimpse, a multimodal model that can crop, re-inspect frames and run code on an image mid-reasoning. The company says it beats larger rivals on scientific chart reasoning, priced at $0.60/$3 per million tokens.

news.title: Nvidia releases open Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120B multimodal model for agents
news.summary: Nvidia's new open vision-language model targets document, chart and web workflows, and Nvidia claims post-trained versions beat top closed models on several domain tasks. Weights are on Hugging Face and other hubs, alongside a smaller 74B variant.

news.title: Perplexity open-sources its SPACE sandbox for AI agents
news.summary: Perplexity is giving away the microVM sandbox it uses to contain long-running agents, and says no frontier model escaped it in red-team tests. CoreWeave, Akamai and Crusoe will offer it to their customers.

news.title: Taiwan to fund up to $4B Texas complex for Nvidia's smaller suppliers
news.summary: Taiwan's economy ministry plans US industrial parks for second-tier suppliers to Nvidia, TSMC and Foxconn, starting with a Texas site, backed by loan guarantees. The aim is to meet trade-deal investment pledges and cut China exposure in AI hardware.

news.title: Jensen Huang says Nvidia would cut off customers building unsafe AI
news.summary: Nvidia's CEO called it a hypothetical but said he would halt chip supply to a customer building dangerous AI. He argued the better fix is faster progress on tools that monitor and contain AI systems, a market Nvidia is moving into.

news.title: Meta's new business terms may let it scrape news sites for AI training
news.summary: Legal experts say terms taking effect Oct 30 let Meta crawl any site tied to a Facebook, Instagram or WhatsApp business account and use it for training, with no opt-out. That would cover almost every newsroom.

news.title: Massachusetts weighs some of the strictest state AI rules in the US
news.summary: The state Senate's economic development bill could require independent evaluations of AI companies' models and safety practices. The bill is still being negotiated with the House.

news.title: Four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft from a random spawn
news.summary: A Google DeepMind paper reports four coding agents, coordinating only via in-game chat and shared memory, defeated the Ender Dragon in about 27 hours. They wrote 2,783 programs and found roles on their own without human-written game tools.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness
papers.tldr: A framework and theory for agents that improve their own prompts, memory, tools, and code around a frozen model, with a rule for when a self-made change is safe to keep.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Once an AI agent is deployed, the work it is asked to do keeps changing. The usual fix is to retrain or fine-tune the model, which is expensive and often impossible when the model sits behind a proprietary API. But a lot of an agent's behavior does not live in the model weights. It lives in the "harness": the prompts, memory stores, workflows, tool code, and control logic wrapped around the model. Teams increasingly let agents edit that harness themselves, yet there has been no shared vocabulary for these systems and no principled way to decide when a self-made change is safe to keep.

## The idea
The authors frame "harness self-evolution" as its own research area. The model stays frozen. The agent studies the results of its own runs, proposes edits to the surrounding software, and changes that get accepted carry forward into future runs. The paper separates *what* gets edited from *how* edits are proposed and approved, and it adds theory for deciding when an edit should be admitted.

## How it works
Each update round collects a batch of rollouts (full task attempts), diagnoses what went wrong, proposes a revision, tests it, and then admits it or keeps the current version. Admission can require a human sign-off. The paper sorts edits into two families. Interpreted-state updates change instructions, stored experience, or task routing while the underlying operators stay fixed; GEPA, AFlow, and ExpeL fall here. Executable revisions go deeper: rewriting component code, changing repository-level control logic such as context building, error recovery, and stopping rules, or swapping which plugins and runtime services get wired together. On the theory side, the authors cast the search over harness versions as evolutionary optimization. They then use continual PAC learning (a framework for bounding how far performance on new data can drift from what was measured) to derive bounds on generalization and on retention of earlier skills, plus a rule that admits a change only if it passes fresh, independent validation data with high probability.

## Results
This is mostly a survey and theory paper, so its numbers come from prior work it collects. On SpreadsheetBench, a harness-optimization method with skills scored 77.58% on GPT-5.4-nano, edging out GPT-5.5 paired with a skill-optimization baseline (76.20%). Across four models it beat that baseline by 5.69 to 11.39 points, for example 85.05 vs. 79.36 on GPT-5.4. In a separate spreadsheet case study, the first task needed only 3 tool calls instead of 13, but used 15.7% more tokens and 54.9% more wall time. Savings showed up from the second task on and reached 110,351 tokens and 22.97 seconds after five tasks.

## Why it matters
For engineers running agents on a frozen or hosted model, improving the harness is the most practical lever available. This paper gives a map of the design choices and a concrete principle: gate every self-edit on fresh validation data instead of trusting whatever scored best during the search.

## Caveats
The bounds only hold under stated assumptions, and the excerpt did not give explicit constants. The benchmark comparisons are borrowed from other papers and are not cost-matched, which the authors acknowledge. Changes to shared context or recovery logic can quietly break parts of the system nobody touched, and interface checks do not prevent that. The authors call for continual validation and independent safeguards, especially where agents can take consequential actions.

papers.title: Agent-Reflex: Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively
papers.tldr: A three-stage training recipe that teaches tool-using agents to notice and recover from noisy tool feedback and user corrections, lifting an 8B model on long-horizon agent benchmarks.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Tool-using agents built on language models do fine in clean test setups but run into trouble in real deployments. Tools return errors, partial data, or misleading output, and users jump in midway to correct course. Most agent training teaches the model to follow a successful path. It does not teach the model to notice that something went wrong, think about why, and recover. So small amounts of noise can push a long multi-step task off track.

## The idea
Agent-Reflex trains reflection on purpose. It deliberately breaks tool feedback during training, compares runs that recovered with runs that failed, and distills the difference into reusable "reflection skills." It then trains the agent to use those skills, first by imitation and then by reinforcement learning under noisy conditions.

## How it works
The framework has three stages. (1) Reflection skill discovery: the team scales up simulated tool environments (557 MCP environments, where MCP is a standard protocol for connecting models to tools), injects perturbations into tool responses, and mines matched pairs of successful and failed trajectories on the same task. From these pairs it summarizes about 1,170 reusable meta-skills, short strategies for spotting and handling failures. (2) Reflective supervised fine-tuning: the skills become training examples covering self-reflection, recovering from a broken step, and accepting user corrections. The released dataset holds about 54K examples. (3) On-policy reflective policy optimization: the agent is trained with reinforcement learning while interacting with noisy environments. This is combined with on-policy distillation, where the agent's own attempts are steered by reflection guidance instead of only learning from fixed demonstrations. The RL set holds about 2K tasks.

## Results
Starting from Qwen3-8B, an 8-billion-parameter open model, the trained agent scores 58.6 overall across five long-horizon tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, a benchmark built around noisy agent interactions. The authors report an 18.4-point overall gain over the base model and say it beats environment-scaling baselines (Agent-World, EnvScaler) and a noise-focused baseline (NoisyAgent). They also report better robustness to noise and stable training across six agent benchmark suites.

## Why it matters
Real agents fail in messy ways, and recovery often matters more than raw success on clean tasks. This work treats recovery as a skill you can train, using a repeatable recipe: inject faults, mine contrasting pairs, distill lessons, then reinforce them. That makes a small open model more dependable in multi-step tool workflows. The model and both datasets are released, so teams can try it or adapt the pipeline to their own tools.

## Caveats
The paper is labeled a work in progress. The results come from one 8B base model, and the noise is synthetic perturbation that may not match the failure modes of your production tools. I could not read the full results tables, so per-benchmark breakdowns, compute costs, and how the gains hold on larger models are not covered here. The headline numbers are the authors' own reported results.

papers.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
papers.tldr: Storing the KV cache mostly in 4-bit, with attention-sink and recent tokens kept in 8-bit, makes RL rollouts up to nearly 2x faster without hurting final accuracy.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains reasoning models by having them generate many long answers ("rollouts"), checking them automatically, and updating the weights. Generating those rollouts takes up most of each training step. Asynchronous rollout helps: instead of waiting for the slowest sequence in a batch, the sampler keeps going and overlaps generation with training. The authors point out a side effect. With asynchronous rollout, each decode step ends up handling more long-context sequences at the same time, so the key-value (KV) cache becomes the bottleneck. The KV cache stores the attention keys and values of every earlier token, and it has to be read on every new token. They call this effect "KV concentration."

## The idea
If the KV cache is the bottleneck, compress the KV cache rather than the model weights. The authors compare options under matched workloads. Quantizing the KV cache (storing it in fewer bits) gave more speedup than quantizing only the weights, or the weights plus activations. The catch is that plain 4-bit (INT4) KV storage changes the sampler's token probabilities enough to hurt learning. This happened even when they used token-level truncated importance sampling, a common fix for the gap between the sampling model and the training model.

## How it works
KV4-RL stores most of the KV cache in INT4 and needs no calibration, so there is no offline step to tune quantization ranges. A small, bounded set of positions stays at higher precision (INT8). These are the "attention sinks," the first few tokens that soak up a large share of attention in most LLMs, plus a window of the most recent context. Those few positions carry outsized weight in the attention output. Keeping them more precise shrinks the gap between the probabilities the fast sampler produces and the ones the BF16 trainer expects. Because the INT8 set has a fixed size, memory and bandwidth costs stay close to pure INT4.

## Results
The main experiment ran 400 iterations of GRPO, a popular RLVR algorithm, on Qwen3-8B-Base. Against BF16 rollout, KV4-RL gave a 1.80x cumulative rollout speedup and a 1.27x speedup for the full training iteration, including the parts quantization doesn't touch. Over the last 50 iterations, when responses tend to be longer, the rollout speedup reached 1.97x. For both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, final accuracy averaged over six benchmarks stayed within 0.5 percentage points of training with BF16 rollouts.

## Why it matters
RL post-training for reasoning models is costly mostly because of generation, and responses keep getting longer. This paper shows that the right compression target depends on the serving pattern: under asynchronous rollout, KV memory traffic matters more than weight size. The fix is simple, needs no calibration, and fits into existing rollout engines. A nearly 2x faster rollout phase in late training translates directly into lower GPU-hours per RL run. The same sink-plus-recent mixed-precision trick may carry over to ordinary long-context serving.

## Caveats
Results cover two Qwen3 base models (4B and 8B) and one algorithm (GRPO). It is unclear how the method behaves with larger models, MoE architectures, or other RL recipes. The whole-iteration gain (1.27x) is much smaller than the rollout gain, because training and other overheads are unchanged. Getting real speedups depends on fast INT4 attention kernels on the target hardware. I couldn't access the full paper text, so details such as the exact size of the INT8 window and the hardware used are not covered here.

papers.title: Joint Subspace Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
papers.tldr: A training-free, token-level sparse attention method that scores tokens in a learned low-dimensional subspace and uses a gather-free kernel, reaching up to 6.43x faster decoding at 128K context.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
When an LLM generates text with a long context, such as 128K tokens, every new token has to read the whole key-value (KV) cache, the stored attention data for all earlier tokens. At that length, decoding speed is limited mainly by memory bandwidth, not compute. Sparse attention addresses this by reading only the tokens that matter most for the current query. Most practical methods choose in coarse blocks or pages, though, which wastes bandwidth on irrelevant neighbors and can miss important tokens. Choosing individual tokens is more precise but brings two problems. Scoring every token cheaply is hard to do accurately, and gathering tokens scattered across memory can eat up the speed gain.

## The idea
Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) chooses at the token level and tackles both problems. For scoring, it projects queries and keys into a small shared subspace that is learned to preserve how tokens rank against each other, rather than simply truncating dimensions. For the memory problem, it uses a custom kernel that computes attention directly over the selected token indices, with no separate gather step that copies them into a contiguous buffer.

## How it works
The ideal subspace would keep the low-dimensional query-key scores as close as possible to the full-dimensional ones. That objective is non-convex and hard to optimize. The authors replace it with a tractable approximation that has a closed-form spectral solution, essentially an eigen-decomposition computed once. They report that optimizing the exact objective brought no measurable improvement. At decode time, JSSA scores all cached tokens in the cheap subspace, keeps the top ones, and runs exact attention over only those. The kernel supports grouped-query attention (GQA), where several query heads share one KV head. Each KV head can make its own selection, so it is not forced into a single shared choice. No model retraining is needed.

## Results
The authors tested three attention designs: standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA, the compressed-KV design used in DeepSeek models). JSSA's accuracy stayed close to full-KV attention on all three. It also avoided two failure modes seen in competing sparse methods: generations growing longer, and breakdowns on specific architectures. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU at 128K context, decoding throughput was up to 6.43x that of full-KV attention. Compared with DeepSeek's model-native sparse attention (DSA), which is built into training, JSSA reached comparable reasoning accuracy without any training and delivered 96-99% of DSA's decoding throughput on 700B-scale models.

## Why it matters
Long-context and long-reasoning workloads are increasingly dominated by decode cost. JSSA is training-free, works across the major attention variants used in current open models, and nearly matches a sparse-attention scheme that has to be trained into the model. That makes it a plausible drop-in speedup for serving existing checkpoints at long context, especially reasoning models whose outputs get long.

## Caveats
The headline speedup is an upper bound ("up to") measured at 128K tokens on B200 hardware. Gains at shorter contexts or on other GPUs are likely smaller. The method relies on a custom kernel, so adopting it means integrating that kernel into your serving stack. The KV cache still has to fit in memory, because this approach cuts bandwidth, not storage. I couldn't access the full paper text, so details such as token budgets, subspace size, and per-benchmark scores are not covered here.

papers.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
papers.tldr: Running the first pass of a looped MoE block on a half-length compressed sequence and spending the savings on a wider model gives lower loss at matched compute, with a predicted 19% training-compute saving over plain MoE.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Looped models save memory by sending activations through the same block of layers more than once, so a model can act deeper than its stored weight count suggests. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models save compute by sending each token to only a few "expert" sub-networks. Combining them is attractive, but every extra trip through the shared block costs the same compute as the first. So far, looped designs have treated every trip as equally important, and no one has checked whether that is true.

## The idea
The authors gave each of the two trips through a shared block its own learnable residual scale (how strongly that trip's output is added back into the running hidden state) and let training choose the values. The first trip consistently ended up much weaker: roughly 0.27 versus 0.87 at 1.3B parameters, and 0.36 versus 1.09 at 3B. Fixing the first trip's scale at 0.25 and the second's at 1 gave lower validation loss than treating both trips equally, while shrinking the second trip made results worse. Their conclusion is that the first trip does a rougher job and does not need full detail. LatentLoop exploits this by running the first trip on a compressed sequence and putting the saved compute into a wider model.

## How it works
- A few normal entry layers process every token.
- A parameter-free mean step averages each neighbouring pair of token states, so the first trip through the shared block sees half as many positions.
- That trip's update is written back to the full-length sequence through learned per-channel, per-position coefficients. These are arranged so that no token can see information from later tokens, which keeps the model causal.
- The second trip runs the same block over every token at full resolution, followed by the exit layers.
- The MoE routers and experts are shared by both trips. Attention gets separate weights for each trip because the two trips work on sequences of different lengths.
- The freed compute pays for a larger hidden size. All comparisons hold stored parameters, KV-cache size, per-step FLOPs and total training FLOPs equal.

## Results
- The team tested 15 configurations between 1.3B and 7B parameters, with the biggest training budget above 10^21 FLOPs. LatentLoop had lower validation loss than both a plain MoE and a looped MoE baseline at every matched point.
- From fitted compute-optimal curves, reaching a validation loss of 1.988 is predicted to take 19.0% less training compute than plain MoE and 7.9% less than the looped baseline.
- In a 3B ablation trained on 40B tokens, compressing only the first trip gave a loss of 2.0199. Using full resolution for both trips gave 2.0293, compressing only the second gave 2.0386, and compressing both gave 2.0467.
- At 7B with 140B tokens, the average 5-shot score across nine benchmarks was 63.40%, against 62.55% for the looped baseline. LatentLoop had the best average in all six size and shot settings.

## Why it matters
For teams building sparse models, this gives a cheap, weight-free way to make looping more efficient: spend less on early, coarse passes and more on the passes that matter.

## Caveats
The compute savings are predictions from fitted curves, not measured wall-clock or inference speedups. The benchmark gains are small, under one point at 7B, and LatentLoop does not win every individual task. The largest model tested is 7B, and only a 2x compression ratio is studied. The authors also say the residual-scale finding motivates the design but does not fully explain why it works.

papers.title: Long-Horizon RL Needs Muon
papers.tldr: A single-rollout asynchronous RL recipe built around the Muon optimizer roughly triples training success for a small coding agent on GitHub-issue fixing compared with an Adam baseline.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Training LLM agents with reinforcement learning on long, multi-step tasks such as fixing a real GitHub issue is unstable and slow. The only reliable reward arrives at the end, when the final patch either passes the tests or fails. Episodes vary widely in length, so it is unclear how much each one should count. Popular group-based methods (GRPO-style) also wait for several rollouts of the same task before updating, which wastes time when each rollout involves dozens of tool calls.

## The idea
The authors put together a practical training recipe for these long-horizon agents and argue that the optimizer choice matters a lot. Their recipe uses the Muon optimizer in place of AdamW, together with single-rollout asynchronous updates and a few stabilising tricks. Muon is an optimizer that roughly orthogonalizes the momentum update for each weight matrix, which keeps any single direction from dominating a step.

## How it works
- **One rollout per task, asynchronous.** Each issue gets a single tool-using attempt, and the policy keeps updating while new attempts are collected. This builds on SPO (Single-stream Policy Optimization) and an improved version the authors call SPO++.
- **Binary outcome reward.** A rollout scores 1 if its patch passes both the tests for the issue and the existing regression tests, and 0 otherwise. Evaluations with empty test sets or broken infrastructure are left out.
- **Muon for hidden matrices.** Embeddings, the output head, norms and vector parameters still use AdamW.
- **Truncated importance sampling.** Token weights correct for the gap between the policy that generated a rollout and the one being trained, and are capped at 2.
- **Token-averaged loss.** Longer trajectories count in proportion to their token count, rather than every trajectory counting equally.
- **Small penalties.** Tool errors and responses over 2,048 tokens are penalised. The combined penalty per turn is clipped to between -0.25 and 0.25.

## Results
The team trained MiniCPM5-2B and Qwen3.5-4B on issue-resolution tasks from R2E-Gym inside the Claude Code harness, with matched update and rollout budgets. The metric is training success: the share of rollouts whose final patch passes all required tests. For MiniCPM5-2B, averaged over updates 90 to 100, SPO++ with Muon reached 74.1%, SPO with Muon reached 45.2%, and SPO with Adam reached 26.8%. The full recipe also beat the baselines on Qwen3.5-4B, although the paper gives those numbers only in a chart.

## Why it matters
Muon has mostly been discussed as a pretraining optimizer. This work suggests it may also stabilise RL fine-tuning for agents, where noisy, sparse rewards make AdamW struggle. The single-rollout asynchronous setup is also a simple way to keep GPUs busy when individual episodes are long.

## Caveats
The title claims more than the evidence supports. The full recipe changes several things at once, so its gain cannot be pinned on Muon alone. Muon versus Adam under plain SPO did not show a consistent advantage across both model families. Results come from selected runs with few seeds, and only training success is reported, with no held-out benchmark, wall-clock time or compute cost. The only task tested is repository-level issue resolution, and the models are small (2B and 4B).

papers.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
papers.tldr: A Hopper attention kernel plus a context-parallel system that uses a compact attention mask to skip masked work, balance load and prune communication, speeding up 128K-context training by 7 to 11%.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Long-context training (up to 128K tokens) almost always uses an attention mask, a rule saying which tokens may look at which others. Examples are causal masks, document masks (packed documents must not see each other) and sliding windows. One GPU can't hold such sequences, so teams use context parallelism (CP), which splits the sequence across GPUs. The mask then becomes a bottleneck: kernels waste time on fully masked blocks, GPUs get unequal work, and each rank must work out its own slice of the mask. The earlier FlashMask stored masks compactly but only targeted older Ampere GPUs and ran on a single device.

## The idea
FlashMask-3 treats the compact mask as information to use throughout the system, not just a storage trick. For each key position it records two ranges of masked query rows, one above and one below the diagonal, in four vectors. That takes linear memory instead of a full n-by-n grid. From that compact description, every GPU can derive its local mask, the kernel can tell which tiles to skip, and the scheduler can estimate how much work each chunk holds.

## How it works
- **Hopper kernel.** It is built on the FlashAttention-3 pipeline, which uses Hopper's TMA (asynchronous bulk memory copies) and WGMMA (warp-group matrix multiplies). Warps are split into three roles. An index generator lists the tiles that have any work. A loader fetches those tiles. A math group computes them and applies the per-row mask only on partially masked tiles. Fully masked tiles are skipped entirely. A persistent scheduler lets thread blocks pick up new query blocks dynamically, because blocks can carry very different amounts of work.
- **Zero-communication localization.** Each rank clips and shifts the global boundary vectors to fit its own chunks. The authors prove the result is exact, and no messages need to be exchanged.
- **Load balancing (HCC-IPO).** Per-chunk cost is estimated from the tile counts, and chunks are then swapped between ranks with awareness of the node topology.
- **Overlap.** Attention starts while keys and values are still arriving. KV chunks that are fully masked are never sent. The all-gather crosses nodes first and then uses NVLink inside each node. In the backward pass, the reduce-scatter is pipelined with the next segment's work.

## Results
- **Single H100, 12 mask types, 4K to 128K tokens.** Attention throughput is 45 to 141% higher than FlashMask, 34 to 71% higher than FlexAttention, and 2 to 44% higher than MagiAttention.
- **Distributed scaling, CP degree 4 to 32.** Throughput is 1.80 to 3.71x Megatron-Core's ring CP, 1.71 to 2.92x its all-gather CP, and 1.09 to 1.46x MagiAttention.
- **End-to-end training.** On a 118B-parameter MoE model (14B active) at 128K context on 128 H100s, training throughput rose 7.3 to 11.0%. In the reported run that meant 902 versus 812 tokens/s/GPU, with attention itself up to 44.9% faster.
- **Ablation.** Removing the dedicated index-generator warp dropped forward throughput to 0.03 to 0.13x of the full kernel.

## Why it matters
Structured masks are standard in long-context pretraining, and their cost grows once sequences span many GPUs. FlashMask-3 shows that one compact mask representation can drive tile skipping, load balancing and communication pruning together. The code is open in PaddlePaddle's FlashMask repository.

## Caveats
Only masks whose masked queries per key form at most two ranges are supported. The kernel is Hopper-specific, routing assumes 8-GPU NVLink nodes, short contexts may not repay scheduling overhead, and the load balancer is a heuristic. End-to-end gains are far smaller than attention-only gains.

papers.title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
papers.tldr: Meta describes how model co-design, analytical GEMM selection and agent-driven kernel tuning brought recommendation training on AMD MI350X to rough parity with NVIDIA B200.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Hyperscalers want to buy accelerators from more than one vendor to control cost and avoid lock-in. But years of tuning on NVIDIA means models, training recipes and kernels quietly assume NVIDIA hardware. Porting code to AMD with an automatic CUDA-to-HIP translator makes it run, but not run fast. For example, AMD schedules threads in 64-wide "wavefronts" where NVIDIA uses 32-wide warps, so kernel tuning doesn't carry over. This paper from Meta and AMD describes how Meta got recommendation-model (DLRM) training on AMD Instinct MI350X to roughly match NVIDIA B200.

## The idea
Don't just port, co-design. The authors give three principles they think apply to any new accelerator. First, change the model and training recipe to play to the hardware's strengths. Second, choose GEMM (matrix multiply) kernels with an analytical performance model instead of slow autotuning. Third, reuse LLM-agent tooling built for CUDA to optimize kernels for the new microarchitecture.

## How it works
- **Use the memory.** MI350X has 288 GB of HBM versus 180 GB on B200. That let them turn off activation checkpointing (recomputing activations to save memory), raise batch sizes and rethink how embedding tables are placed and sharded.
- **Fix hot kernels.** One embedding bounds-check kernel had many threads contending on global atomic counters. The fix was a tree reduction in shared memory followed by a single atomic per block. In a jagged flash-attention backward kernel, gradients are now accumulated in registers and written once at the end.
- **Agentic optimization.** Meta's existing KernelEvolve agent system was given AMD-specific skills. It profiles a kernel, matches the bottleneck to a known optimization, rewrites the code, and checks both correctness and speed.
- **Origami GEMM selector.** It picks tile configurations by modeling compute cost, memory traffic, cache reuse and the chiplet layout, rather than compiling and benchmarking many candidates. The search takes microseconds.
- The changes were upstreamed to PyTorch, Triton and ROCm.

## Results
- Up to 1.5x end-to-end training throughput over a directly ported baseline. Of that, 1.26x came from co-design alone on a feed-ranking model.
- Bounds-check kernel: 9.0 ms down to 2.1 ms (4.26x), now 1.75x faster than B200.
- Jagged flash-attention backward: 32 ms down to 14 ms. MI350X went from 2x slower than B200 to 15 to 20% faster, and that model's training throughput rose 25%.
- The agent succeeded on over 80% of dozens of production Triton kernels.
- Origami reached 93% of exhaustive autotuning's selection quality.
- Across ten production DLRMs on 8 to 128 GPUs, MI350X averaged 101.2% of B200 throughput (geometric mean), ranging from 82% to 130% per model.

## Why it matters
This is a rare public, production-scale account of making a second GPU vendor competitive for training. The playbook is reusable: memory-aware recipes, model-based kernel selection, and AI agents doing microarchitecture tuning. It suggests the CUDA moat can be crossed for at least some workloads.

## Caveats
The comparison holds GPU count and batch size equal, not power: MI350X runs at 1,000 W versus 750 W for B200. Cost isn't compared. Individual models still lag by up to 18%, and MI350X GEMMs are 1.3 to 1.7x slower than B200's, partly because MI350X emulates TF32. Results cover recommendation models, not LLM training in general. Some figures, like the order-of-magnitude cut in development time, are the authors' own estimates.

papers.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
papers.tldr: A small model that learns a robot world model and a policy together in one training stage, so it can act directly or plan about 32x faster than earlier JEPA planners, with much higher success on contact-rich tasks.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
A world model is a learned simulator: it guesses what happens next if the robot takes a given action, so the robot can plan by imagining outcomes. One popular approach is the JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture), which predicts future states in a compact learned feature space rather than redrawing full images. That avoids wasting capacity on pixels, but current JEPA pipelines are built in stages. First you train the visual features and the dynamics, then you attach a separate policy or a search-based solver. The authors argue this has two weaknesses. The features don't reliably keep the information control actually needs, and solvers like the cross-entropy method (CEM, which repeatedly samples and refines random action sequences) need many imagined rollouts. That gets slow as actions get higher-dimensional or plans get longer.

## The idea
LeWAM trains the world model and the policy together, in one stage, inside the same network. Because the model has to predict good actions as well as future states, its internal features are pushed to keep what matters for control. The learned policy then gives the planner good starting guesses, so it doesn't have to search blindly.

## How it works
A shared image encoder (a small ResNet-18 backbone with a projection head) turns camera frames into latent vectors. A "mixture of transformers" predictor has two branches. One predicts the next latent state from clean actions. The other uses flow matching, a diffusion-style technique that learns to turn noise into realistic action chunks, to model a stochastic policy. A regularizer called SIGReg nudges the latent vectors toward an isotropic Gaussian shape, which stops the features from collapsing into something trivial. To plan, LeWAM samples candidate action sequences from its own policy. It then refines them with gradient descent through the frozen dynamics model, minimizing the distance to a goal state. The whole model is about 17M parameters, and it trains on reward-free offline data: expert demos, random play, and mixed-quality trajectories.

## Results
The paper evaluates ten simulated navigation and manipulation tasks, including Push-T, ToolHang, Transport, Puzzle, and Two-Room. Averaged over those ten, LeWAM's visual planning succeeds 93.5% of the time, against 50.9% for the prior JEPA planner LeWM with CEM. The largest gaps are on hard contact tasks: ToolHang goes from 35.4% to 94.7%, and Transport goes from 2.8% to 83.3%. The abstract summarizes contact-rich tasks rising from 28.6% to 89.7%, and long-horizon goals (100 steps away) rising from 10.9% to 46.2%. Planning runs at 52.5 plans per second versus 1.62, about 32 times faster. Probing experiments show that adding the action objective makes robot state and actions easier to decode from the features. Behavior cloning results are reported as competitive, both in simulation and on real robots.

## Why it matters
One small model that can either act directly or plan when needed is attractive for real deployment. Fast planning helps on tasks where a reactive policy alone fails. The result also suggests that training perception together with control produces more useful features than learning them separately.

## Caveats
Most of the headline numbers come from simulation. The real-robot evidence is described as competitive rather than dominant. Baseline seed counts differ (10 for LeWM with CEM, 3 elsewhere), and the comparisons are mainly against other JEPA planners rather than large vision-language-action models. At 17M parameters, it is unclear how the approach scales to diverse, language-conditioned tasks.

papers.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
papers.tldr: A survey that defines robots that plan, monitor, and recover on their own, and maps the field into 17 categories across model, data, environment, and harness.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Robot learning has moved quickly through several waves. First came classic policies trained on demonstrations or rewards. Then came vision-language-action (VLA) models, which reuse large pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions. Most recently came world models and "world-action" models, which predict how the scene will change in response to actions. A newer push goes further, toward robots that behave like software agents: they plan, gather information, notice failures, and change strategy without a human scripting every step. The work on this is scattered across perception, planning, data tooling, simulation, and systems engineering. Nobody has a shared map of how the pieces fit into one working robot.

## The idea
This is a survey paper. Its value is a taxonomy, not a new algorithm. The authors define "agentic robots" as systems where an agent coordinates the work from observations and execution feedback. That agent decides whether to keep going, look around more, revise its plan, or recover from an error. The ability might live in one big model, or in a mix of models, policies, programs, and tools. The authors then sort existing work into four domains with seventeen categories.

## How it works
The paper first traces four connected stages: conventional policies, VLAs, world and world-action models, and finally agentic systems that orchestrate capabilities and learn from feedback. It then lays out the taxonomy:
- **Model**: training, perception, planning, robot control, and adaptation.
- **Data**: collecting robot data, annotating it, and refining it (often with models in the loop).
- **Environment**: reconstructing real scenes in simulation, generating tasks automatically, and benchmarking.
- **Harness**: the software scaffolding around the model. This covers orchestration, memory, monitoring and failure recovery, reusable skills, infrastructure, and layered systems that stack fast low-level controllers under slower high-level reasoners.

"Harness" is borrowed from the LLM-agent world, where the scaffolding around a model often matters as much as the model itself.

## Results
As a survey, it reports no new experiments or benchmark numbers. What it delivers is the organized map above. It also ends with an outlook naming four open areas: fair benchmarking, agentic robotics on real hardware (not just simulation), efficient use of robots and compute, and generalizing across different robot bodies. The authors also say evaluations should separate three things: recovering within a single episode, generalizing to new tasks, and gains that come only from retraining. They add that tests should confirm that skills the robot already had are not lost along the way.

## Why it matters
For engineers building robot stacks, the four-way split is a useful checklist. A capable robot is not just a better policy. It also needs data pipelines, simulated environments, and a harness that handles memory, monitoring, and recovery. The framing makes clear that a lot of current progress is in systems glue, not only in model weights.

## Caveats
Taxonomies are judgment calls, and the boundaries between categories (for example, planning versus orchestration) are fuzzy. The material I read did not give the number of papers covered. The term "agentic robot" is new and broad, and some of the systems grouped under it are still demonstrated mainly in simulation.

papers.title: VideoJev: System One Model for Video Understanding and Interaction
papers.tldr: VideoJev turns video LLMs into fast decision makers that score candidate time spans or answer options instead of writing text, improving temporal grounding and matching QA accuracy at over 100x faster forward passes.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
Video language models are usually asked questions the same way chatbots are: they watch a clip, then write out an answer token by token, often after a long "thinking" trace. That is fine for a one-off question, but it is a poor fit for visual agents or interactive tools that need quick, structured decisions about a video stream: "when does the person open the door?" or "which of these four options is right?". Generating free text for these is slow, and for temporal grounding (finding the start and end time of an event) it is also not very precise, because the model has to spell out timestamps as text.

## The idea
VideoJev, from Nanjing University's Multimedia Computing Group, treats video understanding as a decision problem instead of a writing problem. Rather than generating an answer, the model scores a set of candidates against the video and picks the best one. The candidates can be time intervals (for grounding) or text options (for multiple-choice question answering). The authors frame this as a "System One" model: fast, intuitive judgments rather than slow, deliberate reasoning.

## How it works
The team starts from pretrained multimodal LLMs (Qwen-based backbones) and swaps out the usual text-generation output for a shared scoring head. Given a video and a query, the head rates each candidate span or option by how well it matches the visual evidence, and the top-scoring candidate becomes the answer. Because one head handles both intervals and options, grounding and multiple-choice QA share a single interface.

Two inference tricks target interactive use. Cached inference keeps the expensive visual processing of a video around, so new questions that arrive later reuse it instead of re-encoding the frames. Joint inference packs several queries into one forward pass, so a batch of questions about the same video costs roughly one model call. Two sizes are released: a dense 4B model and a 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active parameters (35B-A3B).

## Results
On three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B raises mean mIoU (mean intersection-over-union, a measure of how well predicted and true time spans overlap) by 6.7 points over its backbone, and VideoJev-35B-A3B by 10.8 points. Forward passes run 2.8 to 3.1 times faster. On four multiple-choice video QA benchmarks, both models roughly match their backbones running in "Thinking" mode, while being more than 100 times faster, since they skip the long reasoning trace entirely. Code and both checkpoints are public on Hugging Face and GitHub.

## Why it matters
Many real video applications, such as surveillance search, video editing assistants and agents watching a screen, need a fast, reliable pick from a known set of choices rather than an essay. VideoJev shows that a standard video LLM can be turned into that kind of decision engine with large speed gains and, for grounding, better accuracy. The shared scoring interface could become a reusable building block inside larger multimodal pipelines.

## Caveats
The reported speedups measure the model's forward pass, not end-to-end system latency, so real-world gains will depend on video decoding and other overheads. The approach only works when answers can be framed as a choice among candidates. Open-ended questions, captioning or explanations still need ordinary text generation. QA accuracy matches the backbone rather than beating it, so the win there is speed, not quality. I could not read the full paper body, so per-benchmark details are not covered here.

papers.title: Beyond Domain-Routed Supervision: Cross-Teacher Guarding for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: Road MOPD uses the non-routed teachers as extra critics during multi-teacher on-policy distillation, so a student LLM learning math, code and medicine stops sacrificing one domain for another.
papers.summary_md:
## The problem
On-policy distillation is a popular way to post-train a smaller LLM: the student writes its own answers, and a stronger teacher scores every token of those answers, telling the student where it went wrong. A natural extension is multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), where each domain (math, medicine, code) gets its own specialist teacher and training prompts are routed to the matching expert. The catch is that all of these lessons are written into the same set of student weights. Teachers differ in style and expertise, so an update that helps math can quietly hurt medicine. Routing separates who gives the feedback, but it does not stop gradient conflicts (updates pulling shared parameters in opposite directions), and one domain often ends up losing ground.

## The idea
The paper, from JD.com's OxygenVLM team and Nanjing University, proposes Cross-Teacher Guarding, called Road MOPD. The key move is to stop ignoring the teachers that were not routed to a given example. Those "off-domain" teachers act as auxiliary critics on the very same student outputs. Their opinions are used both to decide which token-level corrections to trust and to block updates that would damage other domains.

## How it works
There are two parts. First, cross-teacher-guided credit assignment: when the routed teacher flags a token, the method checks whether the other teachers agree. Corrections that several teachers support get more weight, and corrections where teachers disagree get less, so style quirks of one teacher are less likely to be learned as if they were real knowledge.

Second, preventive multi-teacher gradient projection: the auxiliary teachers also produce gradients on the same trajectories, which show which directions in weight space would hurt their domains. The main update is projected (geometrically adjusted) to remove the parts that conflict with those directions. The strength of this projection is tuned adaptively, so the guard does not become so strong that the student stops learning the target domain.

## Results
Experiments use Qwen3-4B as the student across math, medical and code domains. In the high-conflict pairings (math with medical, code with medical), Road MOPD improves both domains over vanilla MOPD, with gains of more than 5 percentage points under high conflict and medical accuracy rising by up to 8.78 points. It also helps in the lower-conflict math-plus-code setting and in a three-domain math-code-medical setup. The paper reached the top three of Hugging Face's daily papers, with about 240 upvotes.

## Why it matters
Labs increasingly build one general model by distilling from several specialist models. This work identifies a concrete failure mode of that recipe, where one domain's gains come at another's expense, and offers a fix that reuses teachers you already have rather than needing new data or reward models. For anyone merging math, coding and domain-expert skills into one small model, it is a practical guard against capability loss.

## Caveats
Results are shown on a single 4B student and three domains. It is unclear how the method scales to larger models or many more teachers, where running every teacher as a critic on every sample adds compute. Code has not been released yet; the authors say it is waiting for internal approval. I could not access the full paper text, so specific benchmark names and the full results tables are not covered here.
